1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's
bishop's fourth square.} Bc5 {The same.} 3. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} Nf6 {The
king's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 4. d4 {The queen's pawn, two moves. (a) NOTE: This
pawn is pushed two steps, for two reasons: the first is, to hinder your adversary's king's
bishop from playing upon your king's bishop's pawn; the second, to bring the strength of your
own pawns into the centre of the chess-board.} exd4 {The pawn takes the pawn.} 5. cxd4 {The pawn
retakes the pawn. (b) NOTE: When you find your game in the present situation, viz. two pawns in
a front-line, you must take care not to push either of them, before your adversary proposes to
change one for the other: which you will avoid, by then pushing forwards the attacked pawn.} Bb6
{The king's bishop, at his queen's knight's third square. (c) NOTE: If, instead of being
withdrawn, this bishop gives check, you are to cover the check with the bishop; and, in case he
takes your bishop, you must retake the bishop with your knight, who shall then defend your
king's pawn. * In the former edition, the author thought it best not to be precise in the
direction of this move, in order that he might have an opportunity of giving several examples,
on the best way of playing the pawns.} 6. Nc3 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's third
square.} O-O {The king castles.} 7. Nge2 {The king's knight, at his king's second square. (d)
NOTE: Great care must be taken not to play the knight to his bishop's third square, before the
bishop's pawn has been pushed two steps; because, otherwise, the knight would prove an hindrance
to the motion of the pawn. * The black, on that move, could take the white king's pawn, and
afterwards push the queen's pawn two steps, which would break the centre of the whites} c6 {The
queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} 8. Bd3 {The king's bishop, at his queen's third square. (e)
NOTE: The bishop retires, to avoid being attacked by the adversary's queen's pawn, because you
would then be forced to take her pawn with yours, which would separate your pawns.} d5 {The
queen's pawn, two moves.} 9. e5 {The king's pawn, one move.} Ne8 {The king's knight, at his
king's square.} 10. Be3 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square.} f6 {The king's
bishop's pawn, one move. (f) NOTE: He plays this pawn to give an opening to the rook; and this
cannot be hindered, whether he or you take.} 11. Qd2 {The queen, at her second square. (g) NOTE:
You should not take the pawn which is offered you, because your royal pawn would then lose its
column; whereas, leaving yours to be taken, you supply its place by the pawn of your queen, and
sustain it afterwards with your king's bishop's pawn: these two pawns united will undoubtedly
win the game.} fxe5 {The king's bishop's pawn takes the pawn. (h) NOTE: He takes the pawn to
pursue his design, which is, to give an opening to his rook.} 12. dxe5 {The queen's pawn retakes
it.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square. (i) NOTE: He plays this bishop, to
enable himself to push afterwards his queen's bishop's pawn: you could, it is true, oblige him
to double a pawn, by taking his king's bishop with that of your queen: but this would make an
opening to his queen's rook: besides, a double pawn, when tied to other pawns, is by no means
disadvantageous; however, the present move will be the subject of a back game, making him take
your queen's bishop with that of his king.} 13. Nf4 {The king's knight, at his king's bishop's
fourth square. (k) NOTE: Your king's pawn being as yet in no danger, your knight attacks
immediately his bishop, in order to take him, or have him removed.} Qe7 {The queen, at her
king's second square.} 14. Bxb6 {The queen's bishop takes the black bishop. (l) NOTE: It is
always dangerous to let the adversary's king's bishop stand on the direct line, which attacks
your king's bishop's pawn; and, when your queen's pawn cannot close that direction, it is
necessary to oppose him by your queen's bishop, and take his bishop, for every other piece, as
soon as a convenient occasion offers.} axb6 {The pawn takes the bishop.} 15. O-O {The king
castles with his rook. (m) NOTE: You castle on that side, in order to sustain and strengthen
your king's bishop's pawn, which you will advance two steps as soon as your king's pawn is
attacked.} Nd7 {The queen's knight, at his queen's second square.} 16. Nxe6 {The king's knight
takes the bishop.} Qxe6 {The queen retakes the knight.} 17. f4 {The king's bishop's pawn, two
steps.} Nc7 {The king's knight, at his queen's bishop's second square.} 18. Rae1 {The queen's
rook, at its king's place.} g6 {The king's knight's pawn, one move. (n) NOTE: He is forced to
push this pawn, to hinder you from playing your king's bishop's pawn upon his queen, which would
give you two pawns in a front-line upon his ground.} 19. h3 {The king's rook's pawn, one move.
(o) NOTE: This pawn is played to enable you to push your king's knight's pawn.} d4 {The queen's
pawn, one move.} 20. Ne4 {The knight, at his king's fourth square.} h6 {The king's rook's pawn,
one move. (p) NOTE: He plays this pawn to hinder your knight entering into his game, and forcing
his queen to remove, which would immediately make an open field for your pawn.} 21. b3 {The
queen's knight's pawn, one move.} b5 {The queen's rook's pawn, one move.} 22. g4 {The king's
knight's pawn, two steps.} Nd5 {The king's knight, at his queen's fourth square.} 23. Ng3 {The
knight, at his king's knight's third square. (q) NOTE: You play this knight to enable yourself
to puth your king's bishop's pawn next, which will be then supported by three pieces, the rook,
the bishop, and the knight. Biv} Ne3 {The king's knight, at the adversary's king's third square,
(r) NOTE: He plays this knight, in order to cut off the communication between your pieces, and
break the strength of your pawns; which he would undoubtedly do, by pushing his king's knight's
pawn; but you prevent his design, by sacrificing your rook.} 24. Rxe3 {The queen's rook takes
the knight.} dxe3 {The pawn retakes the rook.} 25. Qxe3 {The queen takes the pawn.} Rxa2 {The
queen's rook takes the pawn of the opposite rook.} 26. Re1 {The rook at its king's place. (s)
NOTE: You play that rook to support your king's pawn, which would be left in the lurch, were you
to push your king's bishop's pawn.} Qxb3 {The queen takes the adversary's queen's knight's
pawn.} 27. Qe4 {The queen, at her king's fourth square.} Qe6 {The queen, at her king's third
square. (t) NOTE: The queen returns to this square, in order to hinder the check-mate, now ready
prepared.} 28. f5 {The king's bishop's pawn, one move.} gxf5 {The pawn takes the pawn.} 29. gxf5
{The pawn retakes the pawn. (u) NOTE: Were you not to take with your Pawn. Your first Project
laid in the beginning of the Game would be reduced to nothing, I You would run the risk of
losing the Game,} Qd5 {The queen, at her fourth square. (w) NOTE: The queen offers to be
exchanged with the other queen, in order to break the scheme of a check-mate by the bishop and
the ad versary's queen.} 30. Qxd5+ {The queen takes the queen.} cxd5 {The pawn retakes the
queen.-} 31. Bxb5 {The bishop takes the pawn in his way.} Nb6 {The knight, at his third square.}
32. f6 {The king's bishop's pawn, one move. (x)} Rb2 {The queen's rook, at the adversary's
adversary's queen's knight's second square.} 33. Bd3 {The bishop, at his queen's third square.}
Kf7 {The king, at his bishop's second square.} 34. Bf5 {The bishop, at the adversary's king's
bishop's fourth square. (x) NOTE: You are to observe, that, when your bishop runs upon the white
squares, you must put your pawns upon the black ones; or, if your bishop runs on the black, you
must have your pawns upon the white; because, then, your bishop prevents your adversary's pieces
getting between your pawns. This rule is hardly ever to be dispensed with, in case you attack,
and have some pawns advanced; but, in case of a defence, the rule must be reversed, and the
pawns set upon the bishop's colour, NOTE: Here is an example of the above-mentioned note: if
your bishop was black, your adversary's king might get in between your two pawns.} Nc4 {The
knight, at the adversary's queen's bishop's fourth square.} 35. Nh5 {The knight, at the
adversary's king's rook's fourth square.} Rg8+ {The king's rook gives check.} 36. Bg4 {The
bishop covers the check.} Nd2 {The knight, at the adversary's queen's second square.} 37. e6+
{The king's pawn gives check.} Kg6 {The king, at his knight's third square. (y) NOTE: As the

f7 {The king's bishop's pawn, one move.} Rf8 {The rook, at its king's bishop's square.} 39. Nf4+
